case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: A narrower CFAA leaves breach of contract as the live claim. Terms of service still bind, they simply are not criminal.
case.holding: Exceeding authorised access under the CFAA means obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits, not using information you were entitled to obtain for a purpose the owner would dislike.

quoted_in.lawsuit: Ted Entertainment, Inc. v. OpenAI Inc.

live_cases.name: Amazon.com Services, LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.
Amazon.com Services LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It closes the theory that violating a terms-of-service clause is a federal crime, and it is the Supreme Court backing behind the scraping practices that produced most large training corpora.

reading.body:
Van Buren v. United States (2021) establishes that violating a website's terms of service is not a federal crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, a distinction now central to AI training data acquisition.

The Supreme Court narrowed "exceeding authorized access" to mean entering computer areas you lack permission to reach, not using information you obtained lawfully for unapproved purposes. This means a terms-of-service breach remains a civil matter, typically handled as contract violation, but loses its criminal teeth. The holding created legal space for data scraping practices that did not break into restricted systems, only used publicly accessible information against stated owner wishes.

For AI development, this precedent matters because most large training corpora were built on web-scale scraping that violated published terms of service. Without Van Buren's narrowing, such scraping could have triggered federal liability. The decision does not make such scraping legal or ethical, only removes the criminal law enforcement path. Amazon v. Perplexity AI, now in litigation, will test whether this civil-only framework holds when applied to AI-specific scraping and content reuse.

The data does not cover whether breach-of-contract remedies alone (damages, injunctions) will prove sufficient to constrain AI training practices, or whether they will shift to cases where terms of service are genuinely honored or consent obtained.
